newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu stays, troops practise for Hebron deal.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu stays, troops practise for Hebron deal.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu scrapped a U.S. tour and his troops acted out a worst-case scenario in anticipation of a deal to launch Palestinian self-rule in the Arab West Bank town of Hebron.
But Palestinian President Yasser Arafat said on Thursday that Israel and his PLO had failed in late-night talks to close a deal.
"I'm sorry to say that till two o'clock this night we did not achieve any progress," Arafat told reporters in self-ruled Gaza, adding that he was "not optimistic" a deal would be signed on Thursday.

Netanyahu, caught abroad when violence erupted in September, called off a trip to meet U.S. Jewish fundraisers only hours before his scheduled departure on Wednesday. His office said he hoped to advance talks at a sensitive stage.

In an ominous note for the town that has long been a flashpoint of violence, troops preparing for the handover in Hebron ran a practice drill, closing off entrances so that ambulances could evacuate make-believe casualties, Israel Television said.
Peacemakers planned to resume talks on Thursday.

In Paris, U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said special Middle East envoy Dennis Ross believed the sides would need more than two days to clinch a deal. A senior U.S. official said: "We think they probably have a week to go."
The sides are trying to hammer out an agreement for Israel to hand over 80 percent of Hebron to Palestinian self-rule. Some 400 Jews live in the heart of the town of about 100,000 Arabs.
In an interview with Israel's biggest newspaper published on Thursday, Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak warned of "destruction and terror" if Israel mishandled peace moves.

"If the peace process is not conducted on the proper basis, I greatly fear negative results which will catch all of us and bring enormous damage. Disasters. Terror attacks. Suicide bombers," he told the newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth.
In Hebron on Wednesday, Jews gave warnings of bloodshed if Netanyahu carried out the Hebron redeployment.
"What we say today is that there is a potential massacre and pogrom again in Hebron," settler Noam Arnon said, recalling the slaughter by Arabs in 1929 of some 60 Jews in Hebron.
Hebron's Palestinians have a similar fear. U.S.-born Baruch Goldstein, a Jew from the adjacent Kiryat Arba settlement, massacred 29 Palestinians in Hebron in 1994.
Palestinian officials said the sides were deadlocked over Israel's demand that its forces be allowed to enter PLO-run parts of Hebron in "hot pursuit" of suspected attackers.
"The Israeli side still insists on 'hot pursuit'. Therefore we could not agree," said Palestinian negotiator Mahmoud Abbas. "Talks will continue," he added.

Israel has completed many of the security arrangements to transfer the bulk of the town to Palestinian police. But all of the Jews and 15,000 to 20,000 Arabs will remain under Israeli control in the heart of the town, military sources said.
The Palestinians are pushing for a written Israeli commitment to carry out further redeployments in West Bank rural areas promised by the previous Israeli government.
Israeli media said Netanyahu wanted a reciprocal PLO commitment to peace deals and a promise to fight "terrorism".
Netanyahu, a right-winger who in May ousted the centre-left government which signed the Hebron deal a year ago, wants to modify the accord aiming to bolster safeguards for the settlers.

But settler leaders on Thursday blasted Netanyahu's plans as worse than those of the previous government because they would limit Jewish expansion in the town holy to Moslems and Jews as the burial place of Abraham.
The pullout, due to have taken place in March, was put off after Islamist suicide bombers killed 59 people in Israel.
